intro: Open your backpack and read the tags. Your things came from all over the world. Now walk outside. The road, the streetlight and the library down the block were not bought by any one person. We paid for them together.

This unit is about how people work together. First you will learn why people and countries trade. You will see what Illinois sells and buys, and how Chicago moves goods. Then you will learn about taxes, public goods and the jobs people do.
By the end, you will be able to tell an import from an export. You can figure out a sales tax. You can sort public and private goods. You can also make a plan for a job you wonder about.
bigQuestion: How do trade, taxes and work connect us to our community and the world?

words.d: giving something to get something else you want
focusing on making one thing or doing one job that you do well
a good made in one country and sold to people in another country
a good brought into a country from another country to be sold
when people or places depend on each other for goods and services
a tax on goods brought in from another country
money people and businesses must pay to the government to pay for shared services
something many people can use at once, where it is hard to stop anyone from using it
something you buy that you use, so others cannot use the same one
work that one person does for someone else, like teaching or fixing a road
the money a worker is paid for work, often counted by the hour
the skills and knowledge a person has that help them work

Many rail lines, a busy airport and a port meet there

title: Trade, Government and the Community

chapters.title: Trade Near and Far
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do people and countries trade instead of making everything themselves?

story.title: The Backpack Detective
story.kicker: Jada empties her backpack and finds the whole world inside it.
paragraphs: Jada dumped her backpack onto the classroom rug. Out came a pencil case, a water bottle, a calculator, a sweatshirt and a bag of pretzels. Her teacher, Mr. Ortiz, handed her a magnifying glass. "Read the tags," he said. "Find out where each thing was made."

The sweatshirt tag said Made in Honduras. The calculator said Made in China. The water bottle said Made in the USA. The pencils had no tag, but the box said they came from Mexico. The pretzel bag said the pretzels were baked in Pennsylvania.

The class stuck pins on a big world map. Soon there were pins on four countries and two states. "One backpack," said Mr. Ortiz, "and it traveled farther than most of us ever have." Jada counted. Her things had crossed oceans, borders and highways to reach her.
Then Leo asked a question. "Why don't we just make everything here?" The room got quiet. Nobody knew for sure. Mr. Ortiz smiled. "That," he said, "is the question we will answer this month."
story.think: Pick one thing you use every day. Where do you think it was made, and how did it get to you?

lessons.title: Nobody Makes Everything
lessons.mainIdea: People trade because nobody can make everything they need by themselves.
reading: Think about your breakfast. Maybe you ate cereal with milk. A farmer grew the grain. A dairy farmer got the milk. A factory made the box. A truck driver brought it to the store. You did not do any of those jobs yourself.

*Trade* means giving something to get something else. Long ago, people traded goods for goods. Today we usually trade money for goods. You give the store $4, and the store gives you a box of cereal (example price). Both sides get something they want.
Nobody has the time, tools or skill to make everything. So people make some things and trade for the rest. A family, a town and a whole country all do this. That is why trade happens everywhere.

words.d: giving something to get something else you want
things you can touch that people make, grow or buy, like food or shoes

look.title: Make It All Yourself?
look.text: Imagine you must make your own sneakers. You need rubber for the soles, cloth for the tops and laces. You need a machine to sew them. You also need to learn how. How long might one pair take you?
look.prompt: List three things you would need to make sneakers alone. Why is it easier to buy them?

check.q: What does trade mean?
choices: Giving something to get something else
check.why: Trade is an exchange: each side gives something and gets something back.

check.q: Why do people trade?
choices: Trading is a law everyone must follow
Nobody can make everything they need alone
Stores will not let people make things
Money is only good for trading
check.why: No one has the time, tools and skills to make everything, so people trade for the rest.

check.q: You pay a store $4 for cereal (example price). Who gets something they want?
check.why: You get cereal and the store gets money. In a trade, both sides get something they want.

lessons.title: Doing What You Do Best
lessons.mainIdea: When people focus on what they do best and trade, they can both end up with more.
reading: Sam and Rosa are making snacks for a class party. In one hour, Sam can bake 20 cookies or make 5 fruit cups. Rosa can bake 10 cookies or make 10 fruit cups. These numbers are an example.

If each works half the hour on each snack, Sam makes 10 cookies and 2 or 3 fruit cups. Rosa makes 5 cookies and 5 fruit cups. Together that is about 15 cookies and 7 fruit cups. Now let Sam bake for the whole hour and Rosa make fruit cups. Together they have 20 cookies and 10 fruit cups. That is more of both!
Focusing on one job you do well is called *specialization*. After they specialize, Sam and Rosa trade so each has both snacks. Countries do the same thing. Each makes what it does best, then trades.

words.d: focusing on making one thing or doing one job that you do well
a person or business that makes goods or does work for others

look.title: Snacks in One Hour (Example)
look.cite: Made-up example numbers for this lesson
look.prompt: Who should bake cookies, and who should make fruit cups? Use the numbers to explain.

check.q: In the example, who should make the fruit cups?
choices: Both, for half an hour each
Rosa, because she makes more fruit cups in an hour
check.why: Rosa makes 10 fruit cups an hour and Sam makes only 5, so Rosa should make them.

check.q: When Sam and Rosa each specialize, how many cookies and fruit cups do they have together?
check.why: Sam bakes 20 cookies and Rosa makes 10 fruit cups in the hour: 20 and 10.

check.q: What is specialization?
choices: Focusing on one job you do well
check.why: Specialization means focusing on the job you do best, then trading for other things.

lessons.title: Imports and Exports
lessons.mainIdea: Exports are things a place sells to other places; imports are things it buys from them.
reading: Illinois farmers grow lots of soybeans. Some of those soybeans are sold to other countries and shipped away. Goods that leave a country to be sold somewhere else are called *exports*.

Now think of a banana at a Chicago store. Bananas do not grow in Illinois winters. They are grown in warm countries and shipped here. Goods that come into a country from another country are called *imports*.

Here is a trick to remember. Exports EXIT. Imports come IN. The same soybean can be an export for the United States and an import for the country that buys it. Every trade between countries has both sides.

words.d: a good made in one country and sold to people in another country
a good brought into a country from another country to be sold

look.title: Which Way Does It Go?
look.text: A tractor is built in Illinois and shipped to Brazil. A box of coffee beans is grown in Colombia and shipped to Chicago. A soccer ball is made in Pakistan and sold in Peoria.
look.prompt: For each good, is it an import or an export for the United States?

check.q: Coffee beans are grown in Colombia and sold in Chicago. For the United States, the beans are:
check.why: The beans come IN to the United States from another country, so they are an import.

check.q: A tractor built in Illinois is sold to a farm in Brazil. For the United States, it is:
check.why: The tractor EXITS the United States to be sold, so it is an export.

check.q: The United States sells soybeans to Japan. For Japan, the soybeans are:
check.why: An export for the seller is an import for the buyer. The soybeans come into Japan.

lessons.title: What Illinois Sells
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois sells crops like corn and soybeans and machines like tractors to places all over the world.
reading: Drive across Illinois in summer and you see fields of corn and soybeans for miles. Illinois is one of the top states in the country for growing both. Farmers sell much of the harvest to other states and other countries.

Illinois also has factories. Workers there build machines, like tractors, engines and equipment for building roads. Other factories make medicines, chemicals and foods. Many of these goods are exported.

Why does Illinois sell these things? It has rich, dark soil and plenty of rain for crops. It has skilled factory workers. It has good ways to ship goods. A place's *resources* help decide what it makes and sells.

words.d: the things used to make goods, like land, water, workers and machines
a good made in one country and sold to people in another country

look.title: A Field Near Champaign
look.text: Picture a farm in central Illinois in September. A big combine rolls through tall rows of corn. Trucks carry the grain to a tall grain elevator. From there, some of it rides a train or a barge toward a port.
look.prompt: Name two resources this farm uses. Where might the corn go next?

check.q: Which two crops is Illinois known for growing?
check.why: Illinois is one of the top states for growing corn and soybeans.

check.q: Which of these is a resource that helps Illinois grow crops?
check.why: Rich soil and enough rain are natural resources that help crops grow.

check.q: Besides crops, Illinois factories export many:
check.why: Illinois factories build machines like tractors and engines, and many are sold to other places.

lessons.title: What Illinois Buys
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois imports goods it cannot make well or cheaply, like fruit in winter, phones and clothing.
reading: In January, Illinois fields are frozen. But the store still has strawberries and grapes. Many of them are grown in warmer places, like Mexico or Chile, and shipped north. Those are imports.

Illinois also imports phones, laptops, toys and clothing. Many are made in countries in Asia and Latin America. Some parts, like car parts, come from Canada and Mexico. Canada and Mexico are big trading partners because they are close by.

A *trading partner* is a place you buy from and sell to. Illinois buys what other places make well. It sells what it makes well. This way people here get more kinds of goods than they could make alone.

words.d: a good brought into a country from another country to be sold
a country or place that another one often buys from and sells to

look.title: The Winter Fruit Aisle
look.text: It is snowing in Rockford. Inside the grocery store, the fruit aisle is full: grapes from Chile, avocados from Mexico and bananas from Guatemala. The farm fields outside are covered in snow.
look.prompt: Why would a store in Illinois sell fruit from far away in winter?

check.q: Why does Illinois import fresh fruit in winter?
choices: Fruit is not allowed to grow here
Illinois fields are frozen, so it grows in warmer places
check.why: Fruit does not grow in frozen winter fields, so it comes from warmer places.

check.q: What is a trading partner?
choices: A place you often buy from and sell to
A friend who plays games with you
A store that sells only one good
check.why: A trading partner is a place that buys from you and sells to you often.

check.q: Why are Canada and Mexico big trading partners for the United States?
choices: They make everything the United States needs
They do not trade with anyone else
They are close by, so shipping is easier
check.why: Being close makes shipping by truck and train easier, so trade is large.

lessons.title: Chicago Moves the Goods
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's trains, airport and port help move goods between Illinois and the world.
reading: Goods cannot trade themselves. They have to be moved. Chicago is one of the busiest places in the country for moving goods. Many railroad lines meet there. Trains carry grain, cars and big metal boxes called containers.
O'Hare International Airport is one of the busiest airports in the country. Planes there carry people. They also carry cargo, like medicine, flowers and electronics that need to arrive fast.

The Port of Chicago sits on Lake Michigan. Ships can travel from the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean. Barges on rivers can reach the Mississippi River. Roads, rails, planes and ships are part of a place's *transportation*.

words.d: the ways people and goods are moved, like trucks, trains, planes and ships
goods carried by a truck, train, plane or ship

look.title: Which Way Should It Travel?
look.text: Three shipments leave Chicago. One is 50 tons of soybeans. One is a small box of medicine a hospital needs tomorrow. One is 20 containers of furniture going to a city 800 miles away.
look.prompt: Would you send each shipment by train, plane or barge? Why?

check.q: Which way would be best for medicine that must arrive tomorrow?
check.why: Planes are the fastest way to move small, urgent cargo.

check.q: Ships leaving the Port of Chicago can reach the ocean through:
check.why: The Port of Chicago is on Lake Michigan, and ships travel the Great Lakes toward the Atlantic Ocean.

check.q: Why does good transportation help trade?
choices: It means no one needs to work
Goods must be moved to reach buyers
check.why: Buyers and sellers are often far apart, so goods must be moved to them.

lessons.title: The Backpack Map
lessons.mainIdea: Tags and labels show that the things we use come from many places.
reading: Look at the tag inside your shirt. It might say Made in Vietnam or Made in the USA. Labels on packages often say where things came from too. Reading tags is like being a detective.

Jada's class made a map of one backpack. It had 6 things. Two came from the United States. One came from China, one from Honduras, one from Mexico and one from Vietnam. So 4 of the 6 things were imports.

A single good can come from many places. A phone might be designed in one country, get parts from three others and be put together in another. Trade links all of these workers into one *supply chain*.

words.d: all the steps and places a good goes through, from raw materials to your hands
a good brought into a country from another country to be sold

look.title: Where One Backpack's Things Came From (Example)
look.cite: Made-up class example based on the chapter story
look.prompt: How many items were imports? How many different countries are on the list?

check.q: In the backpack table, how many of the 6 items were imports?
check.why: 6 items minus 2 made in the United States leaves 4 imports.

check.q: How many different countries are in the backpack table?
check.why: The list has the United States, China, Honduras, Mexico and Vietnam: 5 countries.

check.q: What is a supply chain?
choices: A chain used to lock bikes
All the steps and places a good goes through to reach you
A line of people at a store
check.why: A supply chain is every step from raw materials to the finished good in your hands.

lessons.title: Depending on Each Other
lessons.mainIdea: Trade makes people and countries depend on each other, which brings more goods but also some risk.
reading: When Sam bakes and Rosa makes fruit cups, they need each other. Sam counts on Rosa for fruit. Rosa counts on Sam for cookies. Needing each other like this is called *interdependence*.

Countries are interdependent too. Illinois sells soybeans to other countries. It buys phones and clothes from them. When trade works well, everyone gets more goods at lower prices than if each made everything alone.

But there is a risk. If a storm closes a port, goods can get stuck. Stores might run short, and prices can go up. Some businesses buy from more than one place, so one problem does not stop everything.

words.d: when people or places depend on each other for goods and services
when people want more of something than there is to buy

look.title: The Ship That Got Stuck
look.text: A big storm closes a port for two weeks. A ship full of bike parts cannot unload. A bike shop in Springfield orders parts but they do not come. Customers wait. The shop owner starts calling other sellers.
look.prompt: Who is affected by the storm, even far away? What can the bike shop do next time?

check.q: What is interdependence?
choices: Depending on each other for goods and services
check.why: Interdependence means people or places rely on each other for things they need.

check.q: A storm closes a port. What might happen at stores far away?
choices: They run short of some goods
They get more goods than before
check.why: If goods cannot move, stores may run short, even far from the storm.

check.q: How can a business lower the risk of one problem stopping everything?
choices: Buy from more than one place
check.why: Having more than one seller means one problem does not cut off all supplies.

lessons.title: Fair Rules for Trade
lessons.mainIdea: Trade is fair when both sides agree freely and follow honest rules; people disagree about how much to limit it.
reading: A fair trade is one both sides choose freely. Nobody is tricked or forced. Labels tell the truth. If a toy says it is safe, it must be safe. Honest rules help buyers trust sellers.
Trade can be unfair too. A seller might lie about a product. A factory might treat workers badly or unsafely. Countries make rules and agreements to try to stop these problems.

Some countries put a *tariff* on imports. A tariff is a tax on goods that come in from another country. Some people say tariffs protect jobs at home. Others say tariffs make things cost more for buyers. People still disagree about this.

words.d: a tax on goods brought in from another country
a trade both sides choose freely, with honest information and no tricks

look.title: Adam Smith on Buying Instead of Making
look.text: It is the maxim of every prudent master of a family, never to attempt to make at home what it will cost him more to make than to buy.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, Book IV, 1776
look.prompt: Put Smith's idea in your own words. How does it fit with why countries trade?

check.q: What is a tariff?
choices: A tax on goods brought in from another country
check.why: A tariff is a tax on imports.

check.q: Which trade is fair?
choices: A seller hides that a toy is broken
A buyer is forced to pay
Both sides agree freely and the label is true
A seller lies about where a good was made
check.why: Fair trade means both sides choose freely with honest information.

check.q: Why do people disagree about tariffs?
choices: Tariffs may protect some jobs but make goods cost more
check.why: Tariffs can help some workers at home but raise prices for buyers, so people weigh it differently.

review.q: Soybeans grown in Illinois are sold to Mexico. For the United States, they are:
review.why: Goods that leave the country to be sold are exports.

review.q: In one hour, Ben can make 12 bookmarks or 3 cards. Kia can make 4 bookmarks or 8 cards (example). Who should make the cards?
review.why: Kia makes 8 cards an hour and Ben makes 3, so Kia should specialize in cards.

review.q: Why do Illinois stores sell grapes from Chile in January?
choices: Illinois fields are frozen in winter
It is against the law to grow grapes
review.why: In winter the fruit is grown in warmer places and imported.

review.q: Which is part of Chicago's transportation for trade?
review.why: O'Hare moves people and cargo, so it helps goods travel.

review.q: A class counts 10 items. 7 were made in other countries. How many were made in the United States?
review.why: 10 minus 7 imports leaves 3 made in the United States.

review.q: What does a tariff do to the price of an imported good?
choices: It often makes it cost more
It has no effect on anyone
review.why: A tariff is a tax on imports, so the good often costs more.

review.q: What is one risk of interdependence?
choices: A problem far away can cause shortages here
review.why: Depending on others means a storm or problem far away can leave stores short.

review.q: Which is the best reason people specialize and trade?
choices: Together they can make more of everything
review.why: When each does what they do best and trades, both end up with more.

chapters.title: Taxes, Public Goods and Jobs
chapters.bigQuestion: What do we pay for together, and how do people choose the work they do?

story.title: Three Things Nobody Bought Alone
story.kicker: A pothole, a library card and a fire truck all have the same secret.
paragraphs: On Monday, Mrs. Kim's car hit a deep pothole on Oak Street. Thunk! By Friday, a city crew had filled it with fresh black asphalt. Mrs. Kim did not get a bill. Neither did anyone else who drives on Oak Street.

On Wednesday, her son Daniel got his first library card. He checked out three books about sharks. The librarian stamped the due date. Daniel asked, "How much do I owe?" The librarian laughed. "Nothing today. Just bring them back."

On Thursday night, a fire truck raced past their house with its siren on. A kitchen fire down the block was put out in minutes. Nobody on the block had to buy a fire truck. Nobody had to hire the firefighters that night.

At dinner, Daniel asked, "Who paid for the road, the library and the fire truck?" His mom thought about it. "We did," she said. "All of us did, together." Daniel frowned. "But I never paid anything." His mom smiled. "Every time we buy something, part of the money goes to pay for them."
story.think: What is one thing in your town that everyone uses but no one person buys?

lessons.title: Money We Pay Together
lessons.mainIdea: A tax is money people and businesses must pay to the government to pay for shared services.
reading: Daniel buys a toy that costs $20. At the counter, the total says $21. Where did the extra $1 go? That $1 is a sales tax. In this example, the tax is 5% of the price. 5% of $20 is $1.
A *tax* is money people and businesses must pay to the government. The government uses that money to pay for things everyone shares, like roads and schools. Paying taxes is required by law.
There are different kinds of taxes. A *sales tax* is added when you buy things. An income tax is taken from the money people earn at work. A property tax is paid by people who own homes and land.

words.d: money people and businesses must pay to the government to pay for shared services
a tax added to the price of things you buy at a store
money a person earns, such as pay from a job

look.title: Sales Tax at 5% (Example)
look.cite: Made-up example; real sales tax rates differ by place
look.prompt: What is the total you would pay for the $40 item? What pattern do you see?

check.q: A book costs $10. The sales tax is 5% (example). How much is the tax?
Which tax is taken from the money people earn at work?
check.why: An income tax is paid on the money people earn.

check.q: A game costs $40 with a 5% sales tax (example). What is the total?

lessons.title: What Taxes Pay For
lessons.mainIdea: Tax money pays for schools, roads, parks, police, firefighters, libraries and more.
reading: Look around your school. The building, the desks, the buses and your teacher's pay come mostly from taxes. In many places, a big share of local property taxes pays for schools.

Taxes also pay for roads and bridges, parks and playgrounds, police officers and firefighters, and public libraries. Money from the national government helps pay for the military and for help for older people.

Government has a *budget*, just like a family. A budget is a plan for how to spend money. There is only so much tax money, so leaders must choose. More money for parks can mean less money for roads. Every choice has a trade-off.

words.d: a plan for how money will be earned and spent
giving up some of one thing to get more of another

look.title: The Town Council's Choice
look.text: A small town has $100,000 left to spend this year (example). The park needs new swings for $60,000. Main Street needs repairs for $70,000. Both are good ideas. The town cannot pay for both.
look.prompt: Which would you choose, and what would the town give up?

check.q: Which of these is usually paid for with tax money?
check.why: Public libraries are paid for with taxes so everyone can use them.

check.q: The town above chooses the swings. What does it give up?
choices: The Main Street repairs, for now
check.why: The town cannot afford both, so choosing swings means Main Street waits. That is the trade-off.

check.q: What is a budget?
choices: A plan for how money will be spent
check.why: A budget is a plan for earning and spending money.

lessons.title: Who Decides on Taxes
lessons.mainIdea: Leaders chosen by voters decide on taxes at the city, state and national levels.
reading: Who decides how much tax we pay? In the United States, leaders chosen by voters make those choices. That way, the people have a say. It is one way a community makes shared choices.

There are three main levels. A city or county council decides many local taxes. The Illinois state lawmakers in Springfield decide state taxes. Congress in Washington, D.C., decides national taxes, and the President signs or rejects the laws.
The U.S. *Constitution* gives Congress the power to collect taxes. If voters do not like how taxes are spent, they can vote for different leaders. They can also go to public meetings and speak up.

words.d: the part of the national government that makes laws, including tax laws
the plan for the United States government that lists its powers

look.title: The Constitution on Taxes
look.text: The Congress shall have Power To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises, to pay the Debts and provide for the common Defence and general Welfare of the United States
look.prompt: Who gets the power to collect taxes? Name two things the money is for.

check.q: Who decides national taxes in the United States?
check.why: Congress makes national tax laws, and the President signs or rejects them.

check.q: Where do Illinois state lawmakers meet?
check.why: Springfield is the capital of Illinois, where state lawmakers meet.

check.q: Voters do not like how their city spends taxes. What can they do?
choices: Vote for different leaders or speak at meetings
check.why: In the United States, voters choose leaders and can speak at public meetings.

lessons.title: Public Goods and Private Goods
lessons.mainIdea: Public goods are shared by everyone; private goods are bought and used by one person or family.
reading: Daniel buys a sandwich. Once he eats it, nobody else can. A sandwich is a *private good*. You pay for it, and it is yours to use. Shoes, snacks and bikes are private goods too.

Now think about a streetlight. When it shines, everyone on the street can see. One more person walking by does not make the light dimmer. It is also hard to stop anyone from using the light. That makes it a *public good*.

Businesses would have a hard time selling public goods. People could use them without paying! So the government usually provides them and pays with taxes. Streetlights and national defense are examples of public goods.

words.d: something many people can use at once, where it is hard to stop anyone from using it
something you buy that you use, so others cannot use the same one

look.title: Sort the Goods
look.text: Here is a list: a streetlight, a pair of sneakers, a lighthouse, a slice of pizza, a fireworks show over the lake, a backpack.
look.prompt: Sort each one into public good or private good. How did you decide?

check.q: Which is a private good?
choices: A fireworks show over the lake
check.why: Once you eat the pizza, no one else can. It is a private good.

check.q: Why does the government usually provide public goods?
choices: Businesses make too much money selling them
It is hard to make people pay to use them
They are always free to make
check.why: People can use public goods without paying, so businesses struggle to sell them. Taxes pay instead.

check.q: Which is a public good?
check.why: Everyone on the street shares the light, and it is hard to stop anyone from using it.

lessons.title: People Who Work for Us All
lessons.mainIdea: Government workers are paid with taxes to provide services the whole community uses.
reading: Many people work for the government. Teachers at public schools do. So do firefighters, police officers, librarians, park workers and bus drivers. Their pay comes from taxes.
These workers provide *services*. A service is work done for someone else. A firefighter does not make a thing you can hold. She keeps people safe. A librarian helps you find the right book.
Some government jobs are far away. Workers at the National Weather Service warn people about storms. Mail carriers bring letters. Rangers care for national parks. Each job helps the whole community.

words.d: work that one person does for someone else, like teaching or fixing a road
a person whose job is paid for by the government, often with taxes

lessons.title: Volunteers and Nonprofits
lessons.mainIdea: Volunteers and nonprofit groups help a community without trying to make a profit.
reading: On Saturday, Daniel and his mom helped at a food pantry. They packed 40 bags of groceries for families. Nobody paid them. People who work for free to help others are called *volunteers*.
The food pantry is run by a *nonprofit*. A nonprofit is a group that works to help people, not to make money for owners. It gets money from gifts, called donations, and sometimes from the government.
Nonprofits include food pantries, animal shelters, youth sports leagues and many museums. Volunteers give their time and skills. The whole community gains, and volunteers often learn new skills too.

words.d: a person who chooses to work for free to help others
a group that works to help people or a cause, not to make money for owners
money or goods given as a gift to help a group or cause

lessons.title: Why Pay Is Different
lessons.mainIdea: What people earn depends on their skills, their education and how many people want that work done.
reading: Why do some jobs pay more than others? Think about skills. A *skill* is something you have learned to do well. Fixing an airplane engine takes many skills. Few people can do it, so the pay tends to be higher.
Demand matters too. If many businesses need nurses, and there are not enough nurses, businesses offer more pay to hire them. If lots of people want a job and few are needed, pay tends to be lower.
The money paid for work is called a *wage*. Say one job pays $15 an hour and another pays $30 an hour (example wages). In an 8-hour day, the first earns $120 and the second earns $240.

words.d: the money a worker is paid for work, often counted by the hour
something a person has learned to do well
how much of something people want and are able to buy

lessons.title: Learning Pays Off
lessons.mainIdea: More education and training often lead to more skills and more job choices.
reading: Education is the learning you do in school and after. It can mean high school, college or a training program. Training can teach a trade, like being a plumber, a welder or a chef.

Government reports show that people with more education often earn more, on average. They also tend to find jobs more easily. Learning new skills is called building your *human capital*. It is like tools you carry in your head.

Education costs time and sometimes money. That is a trade-off. But the skills can help for years. Many people keep learning their whole lives. Asking questions and practicing are ways to build skills right now.

words.d: learning in school, college or a training program
the skills and knowledge a person has that help them work

lessons.title: Planning for a Job You Want
lessons.mainIdea: You can plan for a career by learning what a job needs and building those skills step by step.
reading: A *career* is the kind of work a person does over many years. You do not have to pick one now. But you can start exploring. What do you like to do? What are you good at? What helps you learn?

Pick a job you wonder about, like a vet. Find out what a vet does each day. Find out what training a vet needs. Vets go to college and then vet school. You could start by reading about animals and caring for a pet.

Make a simple plan with steps. Step 1: learn about the job. Step 2: build one skill it needs. Step 3: talk to someone who does it. Plans can change, and that is fine. Every skill you build can help in many jobs.

words.d: the kind of work a person does over many years
something you plan and work toward
